The Association of Licensed Telecommunications Operators of Nigeria has said summoning chief executives of telecommunications companies over poor network services will not resolve the problem, urging the House of Representatives to address infrastructure and policy challenges affecting the sector. The association’s chairman, Gbenga Adebayo, said meaningful improvement in service quality requires sustained investment, effective regulation and an enabling operating environment, rather than sanctions or legislative summonses. He made the position in a statement made available to PUNCH Online on Monday, following the House of Representatives’ decision to reject his attempt to represent telecommunications operators at a hearing on poor network quality. PUNCH Online reports that the House Ad Hoc Committee on Telecommunications Service Quality had, on October 28, insisted that the chief executives of MTN Nigeria, Airtel Nigeria, Globacom, Mafab Communications and other operators appear personally before it by November 4 to explain persistent service failures. It also threatened to issue warrants of arrest against executives who failed to honour the invitation. Adebayo said the challenges affecting network quality included fibre-optic cable vandalism and cuts, inconsistent Right-of-Way charges, multiple taxation, unreliable electricity supply, bureaucratic delays and insecurity around telecommunications infrastructure. They can be useful instruments of accountability, public engagement and policy development. Nigerians are entitled to demand better telecommunications services, and lawmakers have a responsibility to represent those concerns,” he said. Adebayo said the Nigerian Communications Commission had the statutory responsibility to monitor service quality, establish standards, investigate breaches and sanction operators that failed to meet regulatory requirements. “Sanctions alone cannot build fibre networks, provide electricity to base stations, prevent vandalism or facilitate access to infrastructure,” he added. He urged lawmakers to complement the regulator’s work by addressing policy and infrastructure constraints instead of creating parallel mechanisms of accountability. The ALTON chairman also questioned the constitutional basis for the summons, saying the association had written to the committee on October 20 to raise concerns about the exercise of the National Assembly’s investigative powers under Sections 88 and 89 of the 1999 Constitution. He said the association was willing to cooperate with legitimate legislative inquiries but argued that the scope of the summons raised questions about the relationship between legislative oversight and the statutory responsibilities of the sector regulator. Adebayo disclosed that ALTON had filed a suit at the Federal High Court in 2018 seeking an interpretation of the National Assembly’s oversight powers over telecommunications operators, adding that the case remained pending. However, lawmakers had defended the invitation, arguing that the operators held individual licences and should account directly for their services rather than rely on an industry association to represent them. PUNCH Online reports that at the October 28 hearing, House spokesman Akin Rotimi also argued that subscribers dealt directly with individual service providers and should be able to demand accountability from them. The committee’s investigation followed complaints about dropped calls, slow internet connections, failed airtime and data transactions, and inadequate network coverage in several communities. The NCC said on October 20 that operators had compensated more than 75 million subscribers for poor service in 2026 and carried out over 6,500 network interventions during the year. The measures have, however, come amid continuing complaints from subscribers. Adebayo said the objective of improving telecommunications services was shared by operators, regulators, lawmakers and consumers, but insisted that investment would be necessary to achieve lasting improvements. “My message to Nigerians is simple: we all want better service, but better service requires investment, and investment requires an enabling environment,” he said.
